Where it began

Michael Neser was born in Pretoria, South Africa, on 29 March 1990. When he was ten his family moved to Queensland and settled on the Gold Coast, and that is where his cricket took root. He learned the game in junior sides at the Broadbeach-Robina Cats and was playing first grade for the Gold Coast Dolphins by the age of 17.

At The Southport School he was named the First XI's all-rounder of the year twice running, and in 2007 its bowler of the year as well. Queensland picked him for their under-19 side in 2008–09 and gave him a rookie deal with the state team in 2010.

The player

He began in first-class cricket in 2010–11 with four wickets on the opening day of his debut, against Western Australia. Queensland's new Big Bash side, the Brisbane Heat, took him on in the competition's first season, and with the Adelaide Strikers he was named the club's Most Valuable Player in BBL|03. Cricket Australia put him in its Sheffield Shield team of the year in March 2018, and a first one-day cap for Australia followed that June, against England.

His Test debut came at Adelaide in December 2021, during the Ashes. He hit 35 from 24 balls as Australia pushed for a declaration, then struck with his second ball in Test cricket to remove Haseeb Hameed, and later added Dawid Malan as Australia won by 275 runs. A year later he came back into the side and took five wickets in the match, and in the 2025–26 Ashes he took five in an innings at The Gabba, his home ground. Across 5 Tests between 2021 and 2026 he took 22 wickets at 18.91, with a best of 5 for 42, and made 131 runs.

What made him special

Neser was the man Australia could call on when a regular was missing, and he never seemed to need time to settle. A wicket with his second ball, five in a match on his recall, five in an innings in an Ashes Test at home: he made his chances count. He could bat too. His maiden first-class hundred came in the first match of the 2020–21 Shield season.

The hard part was getting a game at all. He was first named in a Test squad in 2018 and sat through several more tours and series before his chance finally came, and more than once he made way when the first-choice bowlers were fit again. His bowling average suggests the waiting was worth it.

Away from the middle

Cricket took him well beyond Queensland: to Kings XI Punjab in the IPL, and to England, where he signed for Surrey and played for Glamorgan. He was part of the Australian squad that won the World Test Championship final in 2023.

And finally

His first IPL match, in 2013, cost 62 runs from four overs without a wicket. He kept at it, and by November 2026 his Test bowling average was under 19. A single bad evening, it turns out, does not tell the whole story.
